 Jane Wickline stars in the viral November 14 pretape about women whose siblings are happy to let them take on everything.
 By Samantha Vincenty Nov 15, 2026, 7:20 PM ET Sister Now Playing 2:48 Highlight Sister 4:10 Web Exclusive Bob Dylan & The Pope 3:19 Web Exclusive Weekend Update: Mississippi's First Black Senator Hiram Revels Discusses the 2026 Midterms Share this on Reddit Share this on Facebook Share this on X Share this by Email Share this by SMS Copy link Add us on Google Key Takeaways
 SNL’s “Sister” sketch starring Jane Wickline and John Mulaney satirizes how caregiving responsibilities for aging parents often fall disproportionately on women.
 The sketch highlights themes of internalized sexism, emotional labor, and the personal sacrifices caregivers make, including leaving jobs, homes, and daily routines to provide full-time care.
 Viewers strongly connected with the sketch’s realism, with many women caregivers praising it for its accuracy.
 Comedian John Mulaney 's seventh time hosting Saturday Night Live brought the fresh New York Musical many were hoping for — but the evening also delivered a less expected viral sketch. The pretaped "Sister" is a razor-sharp assessment of a dynamic common in many families: One in which everyone's all too happy to let a certain sibling handle every single aspect of caregiving for a loved one.
 How to Watch
 Watch Saturday Night Live  Saturdays at 11:30 p.m. ET on NBC and next day on Peacock.
 Stream Now on "My dad means the world to me. So when I noticed him start to slow down, I knew I needed to get him the best care possible," a man (Mulaney) says at the top of the parody ad. "I didn't want to put him in a nursing home, but a private health aide could cost thousands a week. I didn't know where to turn."
 "That's when I heard about Sister," he adds, as an exhausted-looking woman with rolling luggage ( Jane Wickline ) is presented like a new medical product.

 RELATED: John Mulaney & James Austin Johnson are Bob Dylan & the Pope in SNL’s Cut-for-Time Sketch 
 Jane Wickline plays the classic sister who caregiving always seems to fall on 
 "Sister is a live in 24/7 elder care provider that is completely free, and also your sister," Mulaney's character narrates. "Now I don't have to worry about Dad getting the care and attention he needs, because my sister will do it, and I can get back to my life and the stuf f I like to do."
 "I love my mom more than anything. That doesn't mean I want to help her in the bathroom," another grown-man sibling (Andrew Dismukes) says in a testimonial, adding, "Sister doesn't either. But she will, whereas I won't."
 Jane Wickline during the Saturday Night Live “Elder Care Product” sketch on Saturday, November 14, 2026.
 Photo: Jessica Neves/NBC There's no annoying paperwork or out-of-pocket fees with Sister. "Simply text 'Dad fell' to Sister and she will quit her job, break her lease, and move halfway across the country to take care of him," Mulaney's character explains.
 RELATED: Jensen Huang Warned Tech CEOs in SNL's "CIA Meeting Cold Open" Starring Bowen Yang 
 A doctor (Mikey Day) breaks down how it works. "First, years of internalized sexism warps Sister's brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours," he says as a graphic featuring various religious symbols, books and television whirl around an animated woman. "Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her. And that's it! You're done for life. See you at the funeral."
 A viewer called SNL's "Sister" sketch "so real it almost gave me a stroke from rage"
 "Sister" racked up over 1.2 million views on YouTube alone in less than 24 hours after airing live. It was written by frequent collaborators Mikey Day and Streeter Seidell with Simon Rich, a former SNL writer who returned for Mulaney's episode, with "an assist" from Chase Rosenberg. "Dedicated to my sister Heidi," Seidell wrote on X (formerly Twitter). 
 "You have no idea how many daughters feel seen. Just spectacular," one fan replied to his post. Another wrote , "Brilliant from start to finish. Every single moment rang true for this oldest sister. But the fact that it has male writers behind it gives me hope for other people’s brothers!"
 Another simply replied, "Feels like you talked directly to my brothers."
 SNL's YouTube comments were equally golden, with one person deeming it "one of the MOST wicked and spot on SNL sketches ever written." And one of the most-liked comments pulled no punches: "This was so real it almost gave me a stroke from rage."
